prosaic

/proh-ZAY-ik/ - rhymes with mosaic · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Prosaic means plain, ordinary, and lacking imagination.

He christened the rowboat 'Rowboat,' explaining that after forty years as a patent clerk he preferred his afternoons prosaic.

Example

The astronomy column promised the comet of the century and then delivered the most prosaic forecast in the paper's history: 'Visible Tuesday, weather permitting. Bring a chair.'

Prosaic is more precise than 'boring' because it describes flatness of imagination, not of interest: prosaic language plods along the ground, literal and unadorned. A prosaic report can still be useful — it just refuses every chance to soar.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

pedestrian: Pedestrian writing trudges along without lift or surprise — the complaint is about dullness. Prosaic overlaps, but it diagnoses the cause: language that stays literal and earthbound, refusing every chance at imagery. A pedestrian paragraph merely bores; a prosaic one may still inform you — it just never leaves the ground.

unimaginative: Unimaginative is the blunt complaint that no invention went in — no new idea, no fresh angle anywhere. Prosaic adds the texture of the result: flat, literal, everyday wording. An unimaginative plan lacks ideas; prosaic language can carry a decent idea and still plod, word by earthbound word.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

poetic: reaches for image, rhythm, and lift

vivid: so alive with color and detail that it glows

Where it sits · how numbing the ordinariness becomes

plain → prosaic → humdrum

plain vs. prosaic: Plain is honest simplicity and can even be a virtue — milder than prosaic, which begins to accuse the writing of having no imagination at all.

humdrum vs. prosaic: Humdrum goes further than prosaic: past unimaginative into the numbing drone of sameness, the same beige day repeating without end.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — pros-: prose — straightforward speech (Latin prosa oratio)

Suffix — -aic: characteristic of (a form of -ic)

Put it together: Pros- (prose — from Latin prosa oratio, 'speech that runs straight ahead') + -aic (characteristic of) = having the character of prose. Where verse turns at the end of each line, prose walks on in a straight line, so 'prosaic' became the adjective for language — and for lives — that never turn, never rhyme, and never leave the ground.

Use the root in a new word: prose: Judges praised the clean prose of her application essays.

Root Check

Word Choice

critical / measured

Prosaic is the reviewer's polite frown — say it of prose, plans, or lives that never leave the ground. 'Boring' complains about your experience; prosaic diagnoses the thing itself. Against its unit-mates: bombastic language over-inflates and laconic language under-supplies, but prosaic language commits the quieter sin — plenty of words, no flight.
